title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) remains one of the most widely used mechanisms for retrieving status and operational information from network devices.
In this lab, we will use a MikroTik router as the managed device and Python to develop simple network management and monitoring tools.
The lab follows a progression similar to that used by real network management platforms:

Discover which devices are present in the network.
Identify which devices can be managed using SNMP.
Inspect the information exposed by those devices.
Explore their interfaces and other objects available through their MIBs.
Monitor how selected network parameters evolve over time.

Throughout the lab, you will work directly from a Linux system and use both command-line tools and Python scripts.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
4.1 Accessing the Debian Container
Connect to your Debian container (d13-basic-153) through the CyberRange and open a terminal.
Check the operating system and the installed Python version:
cat /etc/os-release
python3 --version
Throughout this lab, the Debian container will act as the SNMP manager, while the MikroTik router will act as the SNMP agent.






Manager and agent



An SNMP manager sends requests to managed devices and processes their responses.
An SNMP agent runs on the managed device and provides access to the management information exposed by that device.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
4.2 Installing SNMP Command-Line Tools
Before writing Python programs, we will verify SNMP communication using standard Linux command-line tools.
Update the package information and install the SNMP utilities:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install snmp
Check that the tools are available:
snmpget --version
Some of the commands that we will use during this lab are:



Command
Purpose




snmpget
Retrieve one or more specific objects


snmpgetnext
Retrieve the next object in the MIB tree


snmpwalk
Traverse a subtree of the MIB


snmpset
Modify a writable object



Do not worry about their complete syntax yet. We will introduce each command when it is needed.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
4.3 Creating a Python Virtual Environment
Python projects commonly use virtual environments to keep their dependencies isolated from the operating system and from other projects.
Install the required package if it is not already available:
sudo apt install python3-venv
Create a directory for the lab:
mkdir ~/p1-snmp
cd ~/p1-snmp
Create a virtual environment:
python3 -m venv .venv
Activate it:
source .venv/bin/activate
Your shell prompt should now indicate that the virtual environment is active.






Tip



Whenever you start a new terminal and return to this lab, activate the environment again:
cd ~/p1-snmp
source .venv/bin/activate

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
4.4 Installing PySNMP
With the virtual environment activated, install PySNMP:
pip install pysnmp
Verify the installation:
python3 -c "import pysnmp; print(pysnmp.__version__)"
Create a file named test.py:
import pysnmp

print("PySNMP version:", pysnmp.__version__)
Run it:
python3 test.py
If the version is displayed without errors, your Python environment is ready.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
4.5 Checking Network Connectivity
Before using SNMP, verify that the MikroTik router is reachable from your Debian container.
ping -c 3 <MIKROTIK_IP>
Replace <MIKROTIK_IP> with the IP address assigned to the MikroTik router in your laboratory environment.






Important



Being able to reach a device using ICMP does not imply that the device supports SNMP. Similarly, a device that does not reply to ICMP Echo Requests could still provide other network services.
We will revisit this distinction when implementing automatic device discovery.


At this point, your environment should contain:
Debian CT
│
├── Linux SNMP tools
│   ├── snmpget
│   ├── snmpgetnext
│   ├── snmpwalk
│   └── snmpset
│
└── ~/p1-snmp/
    ├── .venv/
    └── test.py
You are now ready to communicate with the MikroTik SNMP agent.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
5.1 Configuring the MikroTik SNMP Agent
Connect to your MikroTik router and verify the SNMP configuration.
Enable the SNMP agent if necessary and configure the following community:



Parameter
Value




SNMP version
SNMPv2c


Community
public


Access
Read-only









Warning



SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c communities are transmitted without encryption and should not be considered secure authentication mechanisms.
We use SNMPv2c here because it allows us to focus first on the SNMP data model and protocol operations. SNMPv3 will be introduced later in the lab.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
5.2 Your First SNMP GET
Let’s retrieve sysDescr.0 from the MikroTik.
sysDescr belongs to the system group of MIB-II and contains a textual description of the managed device.
Its numeric OID is:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
From the Debian container, execute:
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
You should obtain a response similar to:
iso.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 = STRING: ...
The exact value depends on your MikroTik router.
Notice that the result contains three different pieces of information:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0  =  STRING  :  value
        │                  │         │
        │                  │         └── Object value
        │                  │
        │                  └──────────── ASN.1 data type
        │
        └─────────────────────────────── Object identifier
This (OID, value) association is the basic information carried by an SNMP VarBind.






Why does the OID end in .0?



sysDescr is a scalar object.
SNMP identifies an instance of a scalar object by appending .0 to the object OID. Therefore, a GET request must use the complete instance OID:
sysDescr.0
Later, when working with tables, the suffix will have a different meaning: it will identify a particular row of the table.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
5.3 Exploring the system Group
The system group is located below:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
Use snmpwalk to retrieve the objects available below this OID:
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1
Identify at least the following objects in the output:



Object
Information




sysDescr
Device description


sysObjectID
Type of managed device


sysUpTime
Time since the management system was initialized


sysContact
Contact information


sysName
Device name


sysLocation
Physical/location information


sysServices
Services provided by the device




Compare sysDescr and sysObjectID.
What type of information does each object provide? Why could sysObjectID be particularly useful for an automatic network management system?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
5.4 Looking at the Protocol
So far, the snmpget command has hidden the actual SNMP message exchange.
Capture the traffic generated by a single GET operation using the packet capture mechanism provided in the laboratory environment.
Start the capture and execute again:
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
Stop the capture after receiving the response and inspect the SNMP packets.
You should find two messages:
Debian CT                              MikroTik
(manager)                              (agent)

    │                                     │
    │ ----------- GET request ----------> │
    │                                     │
    │ <---------- RESPONSE -------------- │
    │                                     │
Inspect the GET request and answer the following questions:

Which SNMP version is being used?
Can you find the community string in the packet?
Which OID appears in the VarBind?
What value is included in the VarBind of the GET request?
Find the corresponding VarBind in the response. What has changed?







Important



Do not capture and analyse dozens of packets. The objective is to understand one request and its corresponding response.
You should be able to relate what you see in the packet capture to the SNMP manager/agent model studied in class.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 5.5 Performing the Same GET with Python
text:
5.5 Performing the Same GET with Python
The command-line tools are useful for testing and troubleshooting, but our goal is to build network management software.
Create a file named:
get_system.py
Using PySNMP, retrieve sysDescr.0 from your MikroTik router.
Your program should display:
OID:   ...
Type:  ...
Value: ...






Tip



At this point, focus on understanding the PySNMP operation rather than building a generic SNMP application.
Identify in your program:

the SNMP version;
the community;
the address of the agent;
the requested OID;
the returned VarBind.



Once the program works, compare its result with the one obtained using snmpget.
Both tools are acting as SNMP managers and should retrieve the same managed object from the same agent.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
6.2 Retrieving the system Objects
Create a new program named:
get_system.py
The program will retrieve the following objects:



Object
OID




sysDescr.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0


sysObjectID.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0


sysUpTime.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0


sysContact.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0


sysName.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0


sysLocation.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0


sysServices.0
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.7.0




6.2.1 Experiment 1 — One GET per object
Retrieve the seven objects using seven separate SNMP GET operations.
For each returned object, display:
OID | data type | value
Measure the total time required to retrieve all seven objects.
Python’s time.perf_counter() can be used to measure elapsed time:
import time

start = time.perf_counter()

# Operations to be measured

elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Elapsed time: {elapsed:.4f} s")






Important



The seven requests must be performed sequentially in this experiment.
Do not use asyncio.gather() yet.




6.2.2 Experiment 2 — Several VarBinds in one GET
Modify the program so that all seven objects are requested using a single SNMP GET operation.
A GET operation can contain several ObjectType arguments:
await get_cmd(
    # ...
    ObjectType(ObjectIdentity("OID_1")),
    ObjectType(ObjectIdentity("OID_2")),
    ObjectType(ObjectIdentity("OID_3")),
)
Display the returned objects and measure the total execution time again.
Compare the result with Experiment 1.

Answer the following:

How many SNMP request messages are generated in Experiment 1?
How many are generated in Experiment 2?
How many SNMP response messages are generated in each case?
Which approach is faster in your experiment?
Why?
Is requesting an arbitrarily large number of objects in a single GET always a good idea?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 6.3 Verifying the Difference on the Network
text:
6.3 Verifying the Difference on the Network
Use a packet capture to repeat Experiments 1 and 2.
You do not need to analyse every packet in detail. Instead, verify the number of SNMP requests and responses generated in each experiment.
You should observe approximately:
Experiment 1

Manager                         Agent
   │                              │
   │──── GET sysDescr ───────────>│
   │<──── RESPONSE ───────────────│
   │──── GET sysObjectID ────────>│
   │<──── RESPONSE ───────────────│
   │──── GET sysUpTime ──────────>│
   │<──── RESPONSE ───────────────│
   │             ...              │


Experiment 2

Manager                         Agent

   │──── GET ────────────────────>│

   │     sysUpTime                │

   │      multiple VarBinds       │
Relate the packet capture to the execution times measured by your Python program.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 6.4 What Happens When an Object Does Not Exist?
text:
6.4 What Happens When an Object Does Not Exist?
We will now examine how SNMP handles errors.
Create a GET request containing several valid objects from the system group and one OID that does not exist.
For example, you may deliberately modify one of the valid OIDs.
First perform the request using SNMPv1.
In PySNMP, SNMPv1 can be selected using:
CommunityData("public", mpModel=0)
Record:

error_indication;
error_status;
error_index;
the returned VarBinds.

Now repeat exactly the same request using SNMPv2c:
CommunityData("public", mpModel=1)
Compare the results.

6.4.1 SNMPv1 vs SNMPv2c

What happens to the complete request when one of the requested objects does not exist in SNMPv1?
Can you determine which VarBind caused the error?
What happens with SNMPv2c?
Are the valid objects still returned?
How is the nonexistent object represented?

Explain why the SNMPv2c behaviour is more useful when a manager requests several objects in a single operation.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
6.5 Sequential Requests vs Concurrent Requests
Experiment 1 deliberately performed the seven GET operations sequentially:
GET 1 → wait → GET 2 → wait → GET 3 → wait → ...
However, SNMP requests are primarily I/O-bound operations: most of the time the program is waiting for network responses.
Create a third version in which the seven individual GET operations are started concurrently using asyncio.gather().
Conceptually:
results = await asyncio.gather(
    get_one(OID_1),
    get_one(OID_2),
    get_one(OID_3),
    # ...
)
Measure the execution time.
You now have three different strategies:



Strategy
SNMP requests
Execution




Individual GETs
7
Sequential


Multiple VarBinds
1
Single request


Individual GETs + gather()
7
Concurrent




Compare the three measured times.
Why can concurrent individual GETs be significantly faster than sequential GETs even though both approaches generate the same number of SNMP messages?
Does concurrency eliminate the network overhead of sending multiple SNMP requests?
Which of the three approaches would you choose for retrieving several objects from one device? Would your answer necessarily be the same if you were monitoring many different devices?







Note



This distinction will become important later in the lab.
When monitoring a single device, grouping several objects into one SNMP request can reduce protocol overhead.
When monitoring many independent devices, asynchronous execution allows the manager to communicate with several agents without waiting for each operation to finish before starting the next one.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
7.1 Using GETNEXT
A GETNEXT request does not ask for the value of the specified OID itself. Instead, it asks the agent for the next OID in lexicographical order.
For example, consider part of the MIB-II system subtree:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
│
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0   sysDescr.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0   sysObjectID.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0   sysUpTime.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0   sysContact.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0   sysName.0
└── ...
If the manager asks for the object following:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
the agent should return:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
Try it from the command line:
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
Now try:
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
and observe the returned OID.

What information must the manager know to perform a GET?
What information must it know to perform a GETNEXT?
Why can GETNEXT be useful when the manager does not know the complete contents of a MIB subtree?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
7.2 Building a WALK from GETNEXT
There is no WALK PDU in the SNMP protocol.
An SNMP walk is obtained by repeatedly asking the agent for the next object:
start OID
    │
    ▼
 GETNEXT
    │
    ▼
returned OID ───┐
                │
                ▼
             GETNEXT
                │
                ▼
          returned OID ───┐
                          │
                         ...
The OID returned by one request becomes the starting OID for the next request.
The process continues until the returned OID no longer belongs to the subtree being explored.

7.2.1 Experiment — Implement your own walk
Create:
my_walk.py
Your program must receive a starting OID and use repeated GETNEXT operations to display every object below that OID.
Test it using the MIB-II system subtree:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
The output should contain lines similar to:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0   OctetString       ...
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0   ObjectIdentifier  ...
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0   TimeTicks         ...
...
Your program must stop automatically when the returned OID is no longer below:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1






Warning



Do not simply perform a fixed number of GETNEXT operations.
A network management application cannot assume how many objects an agent implements below a subtree. Your program must determine when it has left the requested subtree.



Suppose your program starts at:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
and eventually receives:
1.3.6.1.2.1.2....
Why should the walk stop even though the agent has successfully returned another object?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
7.3 Comparing with snmpwalk
Now execute:
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1
Compare its output with your Python program.
Both should traverse essentially the same part of the MIB.






Note



snmpwalk is a convenient manager-side operation. It should not be confused with an SNMP protocol PDU.
Understanding this distinction is important:
SNMP protocol operation          Manager-side operation

GET                              GET
GETNEXT       ────────────────►  WALK
GETBULK
SET
RESPONSE
...

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
8.1 The Interface Table
MIB-II provides information about the network interfaces of a device below the interfaces subtree:
1.3.6.1.2.1.2
Explore it:
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.2
The interface table contains information such as:



Object
Meaning




ifIndex
Interface identifier


ifDescr
Interface description


ifType
Interface type


ifMtu
Maximum transmission unit


ifSpeed
Estimated interface bandwidth


ifPhysAddress
Physical address


ifAdminStatus
Desired interface state


ifOperStatus
Current operational state


ifInOctets
Received octets


ifOutOctets
Transmitted octets



Unlike scalar objects, table objects have an index identifying the row.
For example:
ifDescr.1 = "ether1"
ifDescr.2 = "ether2"
ifDescr.3 = "ether3"
can be understood as:
             ifIndex

               1        2        3
               │        │        │
               ▼        ▼        ▼

ifDescr      ether1   ether2   ether3
ifType       ...      ...      ...
ifSpeed      ...      ...      ...
ifOperStatus ...      ...      ...
ifInOctets   ...      ...      ...
ifOutOctets  ...      ...      ...
The index therefore connects values belonging to the same interface.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
8.2 Building an Interface Inventory
Create:
interfaces.py
Use SNMP to discover the interfaces available on your MikroTik.
For each interface, display at least:
INDEX   NAME       TYPE       ADMIN       OPER
1       ether1     ...        up          up
2       ether2     ...        up          up
3       ether3     ...        down        down
...
Do not assume that the MikroTik has a fixed number of interfaces or that their indexes are consecutive.
Your program should obtain this information dynamically from SNMP.

Consider the following two objects:
ifDescr.4
ifOperStatus.4
What does the .4 represent?
How does this differ from the .0 used in:
sysName.0

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
8.3 From Inventory to Telemetry
Now inspect the values of:
ifInOctets
ifOutOctets
for one of the active interfaces.
Generate some network traffic and retrieve the values again.

Do ifInOctets and ifOutOctets represent:

the current traffic rate,
the number of bytes transferred during the last second, or
cumulative counters?

What happens to their values while traffic crosses the interface?
Could you calculate a traffic rate if you obtained the same counter at two different times?

This observation will be the starting point for the next section, where we will turn SNMP counters into network telemetry.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 9.1 From a Counter to a Rate
text:
9.1 From a Counter to a Rate
Suppose that the value of ifInOctets is measured at two different times:



Time
Counter




\(t_1\)
\(C_1\)


\(t_2\)
\(C_2\)



The average incoming traffic rate during that interval is:
\[
R_{\text{in}} =
8 \frac{C_2-C_1}{t_2-t_1}
\]
where:

\(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are counter values in octets;
\(t_1\) and \(t_2\) are measured in seconds;
the factor 8 converts octets into bits;
\(R_{\text{in}}\) is expressed in bit/s.

The same calculation can be applied to ifOutOctets.






Important



SNMP does not calculate the traffic rate for us.
The agent exposes a counter. The manager samples that counter and derives the rate.
This distinction between a raw measurement and a derived metric is fundamental in network monitoring and observability.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 9.2 Measuring the Traffic Rate of an Interface
text:
9.2 Measuring the Traffic Rate of an Interface
Create:
interface_rate.py
Your program must:

obtain the available interfaces from the MikroTik;
display them to the user;
allow the user to select one interface;
retrieve its input and output octet counters;
wait for a configurable sampling interval;
retrieve the counters again;
calculate the input and output traffic rates;
display the results in bit/s.

A possible execution could look like:
Available interfaces:

[1] ether1
[2] ether2
[3] ether3

Select interface: 1
Sampling interval [s]: 5

Interface: ether1
RX:  2.43 Mbit/s
TX:  817.32 kbit/s

If the sampling interval is 5 seconds, does the calculated value represent the instantaneous traffic rate at the moment of the second measurement?
What does it actually represent?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
9.3 Sampling Interval
The sampling interval determines how often the monitoring system retrieves the counters.
Consider two extreme cases:
Short sampling interval

C1 ── C2 ── C3 ── C4 ── C5 ── C6
│     │     │     │     │     │
└─1s──┴─1s──┴─1s──┴─1s──┴─1s──┘

More detail
More SNMP requests


Long sampling interval

C1 ─────────────────── C2
│                      │
└──────── 60 s ────────┘

Less detail
Fewer SNMP requests

Compare sampling intervals of:
1 s
10 s
60 s
5 min
What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
Would you use the same sampling interval to monitor 5 interfaces and 50,000 interfaces?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
9.4 Continuous Monitoring
Modify interface_rate.py so that it continuously monitors the selected interface.
After the first measurement, you do not need to retrieve two completely new samples for every rate calculation.
Instead:
C1        C2        C3        C4        C5
│         │         │         │         │
└── Δ1 ───┘         │         │         │
          └── Δ2 ───┘         │         │
                    └── Δ3 ───┘         │
                              └── Δ4 ───┘
Each new counter value becomes the previous value for the next calculation.
Display one measurement per sampling interval:
TIME       RX              TX
14:32:05   1.24 Mbit/s     340.1 kbit/s
14:32:10   2.81 Mbit/s     512.4 kbit/s
14:32:15   950.2 kbit/s    1.13 Mbit/s
...
Stop the monitor using Ctrl+C.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
9.5 Counter Size Matters
The original MIB-II interface table defines:
ifInOctets
ifOutOctets
as 32-bit counters.
A 32-bit unsigned counter can represent values from:
\[
0
\quad\text{to}\quad
2^{32}-1
\]
After reaching its maximum value, the counter wraps around.
Consider a continuously busy 1 Gbit/s interface.

Calculate approximately how long it would take a 32-bit octet counter to wrap around at 1 Gbit/s.
Is this a problem if the monitoring system samples the interface every 5 minutes?

For higher-capacity interfaces, IF-MIB provides 64-bit counters:
ifHCInOctets
ifHCOutOctets
where HC stands for High Capacity.
Whenever they are available, these counters are generally preferable for traffic monitoring.






Note



A robust monitoring application should not simply assume that:
new_counter >= old_counter
A counter may become smaller because of:

counter wraparound;
device or interface restart;
agent restart.

Production monitoring systems must account for these situations.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
9.6 Using High-Capacity Counters
Check whether your MikroTik exposes:
ifHCInOctets
ifHCOutOctets
for the selected interface.
Modify your monitor to use the 64-bit counters when they are available.

What ASN.1/SNMP data type is returned for ifInOctets?
What type is returned for ifHCInOctets?
How many bits does each counter use?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
9.7 Interface Utilization
A traffic rate becomes easier to interpret when it is compared with the capacity of the interface.
If the nominal interface speed is \(S\), the utilization can be calculated as:
\[
U_{\text{in}} =
100\frac{R_{\text{in}}}{S}
\]
and:
\[
U_{\text{out}} =
100\frac{R_{\text{out}}}{S}
\]
Retrieve the appropriate interface speed information through SNMP and extend your program to display utilization.
For example:
TIME       RX             RX UTIL.    TX             TX UTIL.
14:32:05   1.24 Mbit/s      1.24%    340.1 kbit/s      0.34%
14:32:10   2.81 Mbit/s      2.81%    512.4 kbit/s      0.51%
14:32:15   950.2 kbit/s     0.95%    1.13 Mbit/s       1.13%

Does the nominal speed reported by an interface necessarily represent the amount of bandwidth actually available to an application?
Why is interface utilization nevertheless a useful management metric?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
10.1 Concurrent Polling with asyncio
Modify your program so that it can monitor several interfaces concurrently.
Use the asynchronous concepts introduced in the Python class:
await asyncio.gather(
    poll_interface(...),
    poll_interface(...),
    poll_interface(...),
)
Conceptually:
Sequential

A: request ───── response
                      B: request ───── response
                                            C: request ───── response


Concurrent

A: request ───────────────── response
B: request ─────────── response
C: request ───────────────────── response
The program can use the time spent waiting for one network response to process or wait for others.

Does asyncio make the MikroTik answer an individual SNMP request faster?
If not, why can it significantly reduce the total time required to poll many independent objects or devices?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
10.2 Final Monitor
Your final program for this section should allow the user to select one or more interfaces and continuously display:

interface name;
operational status;
input traffic rate;
output traffic rate;
input utilization;
output utilization.

Use high-capacity counters when available.
The program should update the measurements periodically without requiring user interaction.
At this point, you have built the fundamental data collection loop used by a network monitoring system:
       POLL
        │
        ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Read counters   │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Calculate rates │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Interpret data  │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
       WAIT
         │
         └──────────────► POLL AGAIN
In later labs, the same general idea will be extended from individual SNMP measurements to a complete telemetry and observability platform.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 11.1 Discovering Hosts on a Local Network
text:
11.1 Discovering Hosts on a Local Network
If the manager is directly connected to an IPv4 LAN, ARP provides a useful mechanism for discovering active hosts.
The manager can send an ARP request asking:
Who has 192.168.153.1?
Who has 192.168.153.2?
Who has 192.168.153.3?
...
A device using one of those addresses can reply with its MAC address:
Manager                                  Device

   │                                       │
   │── ARP: Who has 192.168.153.10? ─────>│
   │                                       │
   │<── ARP: 192.168.153.10 is at MAC ────│
   │                                       │
This provides two useful pieces of inventory information:
IP address  ↔  MAC address






Note



ARP discovery only works for devices in the same Layer-2 broadcast domain.
Routers do not normally forward ARP requests. Therefore, a management platform cannot use ARP alone to discover arbitrary remote networks.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
11.2 ARP Discovery with Scapy
For this experiment, we will use Scapy, a Python library for creating, sending, receiving, and inspecting network packets.
We will only use a very small part of Scapy. The objective of this lab is not to learn the complete library, but to use it to implement the discovery mechanism discussed above.
Install Scapy inside your virtual environment:
pip install scapy

11.2.1 Building Packets with Scapy
Scapy represents network protocols as Python objects.
For example:
from scapy.all import ARP

packet = ARP(
    pdst="192.168.153.10"
)
creates an ARP packet asking about the IPv4 address 192.168.153.10.
You can inspect the packet using:
packet.show()
Try it.

Find the following fields in the output:

operation (op);
target protocol address (pdst);
sender protocol address (psrc);
target hardware address (hwdst).

What values has Scapy automatically selected for the fields that you did not specify?



11.2.2 Ethernet and ARP
ARP requests are transmitted inside Ethernet frames.
An ARP request intended for all hosts on the LAN therefore uses the Ethernet broadcast address:
ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
In Scapy, an Ethernet frame can be created with:
from scapy.all import Ether

ethernet = Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
Scapy uses the / operator to encapsulate one protocol inside another:
packet = ethernet / ARP(pdst="192.168.153.10")
This represents:
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Ethernet                    │
│ dst = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff     │
│                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│   │ ARP                 │   │
│   │                     │   │
│   │ Who has             │   │
│   │ 192.168.153.10?     │   │
│   └─────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
Inspect the complete packet:
packet.show()
Notice that / does not mean division in this context. Scapy overloads the operator to construct a protocol stack.


11.2.3 Sending and Receiving Packets
Scapy provides several functions for sending packets.
Because we are working directly with Ethernet frames, we will use srp():
from scapy.all import srp

answered, unanswered = srp(
    packet,
    timeout=2,
    verbose=False
)
srp() means approximately:
send and receive packets at Layer 2
and returns two collections:
answered
unanswered
Each item in answered contains both:
packet sent  →  packet received
For an ARP response, the received packet provides the information we need:
for sent, received in answered:
    print(received.psrc)
    print(received.hwsrc)
where:
psrc   → source protocol address → IPv4 address
hwsrc  → source hardware address → MAC address






Scapy and asyncio



The srp() function used here is a blocking operation.
Calling it from an async function does not automatically make it asynchronous:
async def discover():
    answered, unanswered = srp(...)
While srp() is running, the Python asyncio event loop cannot execute other tasks.
For this exercise, this is not a problem. Scapy sends the ARP probes and collects their responses as a single discovery operation:
                    ARP discovery
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     host 1            host 2            host 3
       │                 │                 │
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ▼
                    ARP responses
We will therefore perform ARP discovery with Scapy first and then use asyncio for the SNMP queries:
        Scapy ARP discovery
               │
               ▼
       discovered hosts
               │
       ┌───────┼───────┐
       ▼       ▼       ▼
     host 1  host 2  host 3
       │       │       │
       └── concurrent ─┘
          SNMP queries
           (asyncio)
This also illustrates an important Python concept:

asyncio provides concurrency only when the operations being called are asynchronous and yield control while they are waiting.





11.2.4 Discovering a Complete Subnet
Scapy also accepts a network in CIDR notation as the destination of an ARP request.
For example:
ARP(pdst="192.168.153.0/24")
represents ARP requests for the addresses in that subnet.
Therefore, the basic discovery operation can be constructed as:
from scapy.all import ARP, Ether, srp

network = "192.168.153.0/24"

packet = (
    Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
    / ARP(pdst=network)
)

answered, unanswered = srp(
    packet,
    timeout=2,
    verbose=False
)

Before continuing, make sure you can explain each part of:
Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff") / ARP(pdst=network)
In particular:

Why is the Ethernet destination address a broadcast address?
Why can the ARP destination contain a /24 network rather than a single address?
What does / mean in Scapy?
Why are we using srp() rather than simply sending the packets?




11.2.5 Exercise — Build the Host Inventory
Create:
discover.py
Using the previous example as a starting point, process the responses and produce a table containing the discovered IP and MAC addresses:
IP ADDRESS          MAC ADDRESS
192.168.153.1       48:a9:8a:...
192.168.153.4       02:42:ac:...
192.168.153.17      bc:24:11:...
...
Do not copy the example blindly. You should understand how the Ethernet frame, the ARP request, srp(), and the returned responses work before constructing the inventory.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 11.3 ARP Is Not the Only Discovery Mechanism
text:
11.3 ARP Is Not the Only Discovery Mechanism
Network discovery does not rely on a single universal mechanism.
Depending on the network and the information available, management systems may combine different sources such as:
ARP / neighbour tables
ICMP probes
SNMP
LLDP/CDP
routing information
DHCP information
DNS
traffic observation
...
For example, ICMP Echo Requests can also be used to probe IP addresses:
Manager                           Device

   │── ICMP Echo Request ────────>│
   │<── ICMP Echo Reply ──────────│
However:






Warning



No response to an ICMP Echo Request does not necessarily mean that no device exists at that address.
ICMP may be filtered while other protocols, including SNMP, remain reachable.


For this lab, ARP will be used for initial discovery because the devices being discovered are on the local laboratory network.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 11.4 From a Host to a Managed Device
text:
11.4 From a Host to a Managed Device
Finding an IP address does not tell us whether the device can be managed using SNMP.
For every host discovered using ARP, send an SNMPv2c GET request for:
sysName.0
using the community:
public
If the device provides a valid SNMP response, classify it as an SNMP-enabled device.
Your inventory should now distinguish:
IP ADDRESS          MAC ADDRESS          SNMP
192.168.153.1       48:a9:8a:...         yes
192.168.153.4       02:42:ac:...         no
192.168.153.17      bc:24:11:...         yes

A host was discovered using ARP but does not answer the SNMP request.
Can you conclude that the device does not support SNMP?
What other explanations are possible?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
11.5 Identifying SNMP Devices
For each device that responds to SNMP, retrieve:
sysName.0
sysDescr.0
sysObjectID.0
Extend the inventory:
192.168.153.1
    MAC:          48:a9:8a:...
    SNMP:         yes
    Name:         router01
    Description:  RouterOS ...
    Object ID:    1.3.6.1.4.1....

192.168.153.4
    MAC:          02:42:ac:...
    SNMP:         no
The three SNMP objects provide different information:

sysName provides the configured name of the device;
sysDescr provides a textual description of the system;
sysObjectID identifies the type of device according to the vendor’s object hierarchy.


Which of these objects would be the most appropriate for software that needs to automatically determine what type of device it has discovered?
Why is parsing sysDescr text generally less robust?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
11.6 Enterprise OIDs
Inspect the sysObjectID returned by your MikroTik.
Vendor-specific objects are located below:
1.3.6.1.4.1
This part of the OID tree is known as:
private.enterprises
Each registered organization receives an enterprise number.
Conceptually:
1.3.6.1.4.1
      │
      └── enterprises
             │
             ├── vendor A
             ├── vendor B
             ├── vendor C
             │      │
             │      └── products...
             └── ...
Identify the enterprise number contained in the sysObjectID returned by your MikroTik.






Note



This is one of the mechanisms that a network management platform can use after discovery to decide which vendor-specific MIBs, monitoring templates, or collection rules should be applied to a device.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
section: 11.7 Why Sequential Discovery Does Not Scale
text:
11.7 Why Sequential Discovery Does Not Scale
Suppose several devices have been discovered:
192.168.153.1
192.168.153.2
192.168.153.3
...
A sequential SNMP probe behaves approximately as:
Device 1: request ───── wait ───── response
                                     │
Device 2:                            request ───── wait ───── response
                                                                  │
Device 3:                                                         ...
This becomes particularly inefficient when a device does not respond.
The manager must wait for the SNMP timeout before moving to the next device.

Assume an SNMP timeout of 1 second.
Approximately how long could a sequential scan of 100 addresses take if none of them responds?
What happens if those requests can be performed concurrently?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
11.8 Concurrent SNMP Discovery
Modify the SNMP phase of discover.py to probe discovered hosts concurrently using asyncio.
Conceptually:
results = await asyncio.gather(
    probe_snmp("192.168.153.1"),
    probe_snmp("192.168.153.2"),
    probe_snmp("192.168.153.3"),
    # ...
)
The discovery process now becomes:
ARP discovery
     │
     ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────┐
│  IP1   IP2   IP3   IP4   IP5 ... │
└───┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┘
    │     │     │     │     │
    └─────┴── concurrent SNMP ──────┘
                  │
                  ▼
           SNMP responders
                  │
                  ▼
          Device information
Measure the time required for:

sequential SNMP probing;
concurrent SNMP probing.

Compare the results.

Why is concurrency particularly valuable when some devices do not respond?
Does concurrent discovery generate less network traffic than sequential discovery?
What resource or network problems could arise if a management platform started tens of thousands of discovery requests simultaneously?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
11.9 Building the Device Inventory
Your final discover.py program should automatically:

discover active devices on the local network;
obtain their IP and MAC addresses;
determine which devices respond to SNMP;
retrieve sysName, sysDescr, and sysObjectID from SNMP-enabled devices;
display the resulting inventory.

A possible result is:
Network discovery: 192.168.153.0/24

Discovered: 6 devices
SNMP-enabled: 2 devices

IP ADDRESS       MAC ADDRESS        SNMP   NAME        DESCRIPTION
192.168.153.1    48:a9:8a:...       yes    router01    RouterOS ...
192.168.153.4    02:42:ac:...       no     -           -
192.168.153.8    bc:24:11:...       yes    switch01    ...
...
You have now implemented a simplified version of an important function provided by many network management platforms:
DISCOVERY
    ↓
IDENTIFICATION
    ↓
INVENTORY
    ↓
MONITORING
The next step after discovering and identifying a device would be to determine what should be monitored on that device.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
12.1 Read and Write Access
For the previous exercises, the MikroTik SNMP agent was configured with a read-only community:
public
This is sufficient for monitoring, but it should not allow configuration changes.
Try to modify sysLocation.0 using the read-only community.
For example, with the Net-SNMP command-line tools:
snmpset -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> \
  1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0 s "Network Management Lab"
Here:
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0    → sysLocation.0
s                      → OCTET STRING
"Network Management Lab" → new value
Observe the result.

Was the operation accepted?
Why should a community used by a monitoring system normally have read-only access?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
12.2 Enabling Write Access
Configure a separate SNMP community on the MikroTik with write access.
Do not modify the read-only public community.
Use the write community only for this part of the lab.






Warning



A read-write SNMP community provides the ability to modify writable managed objects on the device.
It should therefore not be used for routine monitoring.


Repeat the SET operation using the write community.
Then verify the result independently with a GET:
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> \
  1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0
The complete operation is therefore:
       write community                 read community

Manager ─────── SET ───────► Agent ◄────── GET ─────── Manager
              │                │
              │                ▼
              │          sysLocation.0
              │                │
              └── changes ─────┘

Why is it useful to verify the result using a separate GET rather than assuming that the configuration has changed because a SET request was sent?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
12.3 Performing a SET with PySNMP
Create:
set_location.py
The program must receive a new location as an argument:
python set_location.py "Lab 1 - EINA"
and modify:
sysLocation.0
using SNMP.
After performing the SET, retrieve the object again and display its new value.
Your program should produce output similar to:
Previous location: ...
Setting location...
New location: Lab 1 - EINA

Compare GET and SET in your Python programs.
Which elements are common to both operations?
What changes?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
12.4 Inspecting an SNMP SET
Capture one successful SET operation.
Identify:

the SNMP version;
the community;
the PDU type;
the OID being modified;
the new value;
the agent response.

Pay particular attention to the community string.






A Security Problem



In SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, the community string is transmitted without encryption.
Anyone able to capture the traffic may be able to obtain the community used for the SET operation.
A captured read-write community is particularly dangerous because it may allow an attacker to modify the device configuration.



Compare the packet capture of your earlier SNMP GET using public with this SET operation.
Can you identify both community strings in the captured packets?
Would you consider SNMPv2c appropriate for management traffic crossing an untrusted network?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
12.5 Monitoring vs Configuration
SNMP can therefore be used for both:
                  SNMP
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ▼                 ▼
        READ              WRITE
          │                 │
   GET / GETNEXT           SET
   GETBULK / WALK           │
          │                 ▼
          ▼             Configuration
      Monitoring
      Telemetry
In this course, our main use of SNMP will be monitoring and telemetry.
Modern network automation frequently uses other mechanisms for configuration, while SNMP remains widely used for retrieving operational state and metrics.
Nevertheless, understanding SET is important because it demonstrates that the SNMP management model was designed for both monitoring and control.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
13.1 The Problem with Community-Based SNMP
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use a community string as a simple access-control mechanism.
Conceptually:
             "public"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             GET

          "write-community"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             SET
The community identifies the access rights associated with the request.
However, the community itself is transmitted without encryption.
As you observed in the packet capture:
Network observer
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: public        │
│ PDU: GET                 │
│ OID: ...                 │
└──────────────────────────┘
and, even more critically:
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: ********      │
│ PDU: SET                 │
│ OID: sysLocation.0       │
│ Value: ...               │
└──────────────────────────┘

What could an attacker do after capturing a valid read-write community?
Would choosing a very long and random community string solve the packet-capture problem? Why?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
14.1 Configuring an SNMPv3 User
Configure an SNMPv3 user on your MikroTik for this experiment.
Use:
Security level: authPriv
and the authentication and privacy credentials assigned for your laboratory environment.






Warning



Do not reuse personal passwords.
The credentials used in this exercise are laboratory credentials and should only be used inside the CyberRange.


Your configuration requires several pieces of information:
SNMPv3 user
    │
    ├── username
    │
    ├── authentication protocol
    │       └── authentication password
    │
    └── privacy protocol
            └── privacy password
Verify that SNMPv3 access is enabled before continuing.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
14.2 Your First SNMPv3 GET
Use the Net-SNMP command-line tools to retrieve:
sysUpTime.0
using SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy.
The command has the following general structure:
snmpget -v3 \
  -l authPriv \
  -u <USERNAME> \
  -a <AUTH_PROTOCOL> \
  -A '<AUTH_PASSWORD>' \
  -x <PRIV_PROTOCOL> \
  -X '<PRIV_PASSWORD>' \
  <MIKROTIK_IP> \
  1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
where:
-v3   SNMP version 3
-l    security level
-u    username
-a    authentication protocol
-A    authentication password
-x    privacy protocol
-X    privacy password

Compare this command with the SNMPv2c equivalent:
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
What information has replaced the community string?

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
14.3 Inspecting SNMPv3 on the Network
Capture the SNMPv3 GET request and its response.
Compare them with the SNMPv2c GET captured earlier.
Try to identify:

the SNMP version;
the SNMPv3 username;
the authentication-related information;
the encrypted portion of the message.

Then try to locate:
sysUpTime.0
and its returned value in the packet capture.

Can you read the requested OID as easily as you could with SNMPv2c?
Can you read the returned value?
Can you find the authentication password in the packet?
Can you find the privacy password?
Can you find the SNMPv3 username?







Important



Encryption does not mean that the complete network packet becomes invisible.
An observer can still see information required to transport and process the packet, such as IP addresses, UDP ports and some SNMPv3 metadata.
With authPriv, however, the protected SNMP scoped PDU is encrypted.

title: Lab 1 — SNMP and Python
text:
14.4 SNMPv3 with PySNMP
Create:
get_v3.py
Modify one of your previous GET programs so that it retrieves:
sysUpTime.0
using SNMPv3 with authPriv.
In PySNMP, SNMPv3 user-based security is configured using UsmUserData instead of CommunityData.
Conceptually:
CommunityData(...)
becomes:
UsmUserData(
    username,
    authKey=...,
    privKey=...,
    authProtocol=...,
    privProtocol=...
)
Use the authentication and privacy protocols configured on your MikroTik.

Look at the rest of your previous PySNMP GET program.
Apart from the security configuration, how much of the SNMP operation has changed?
What does this tell you about the separation between:
what we want to retrieve
and:
how the SNMP communication is secured
